In the context of artificial intelligence, MCP stands for the Model Context Protocol.

Introduced as an open-source standard by Anthropic, MCP is designed to solve a major problem in AI development: information silos. It acts as a "universal adapter" (similar to how a USB-C cable standardizes hardware connections) allowing Large Language Models (LLMs) to securely connect with external data sources, developer environments, local files, and enterprise software.

The Problem It Solves: The $N \times M$ Nightmare

Before MCP, if you wanted an AI model to interact with a specific tool (like GitHub, a Postgres database, or Slack), developers had to write custom, vendor-specific integration code for each pairing. If you had $N$ different AI models and $M$ different data sources, you ended up needing a messy web of $N \times M$ custom connections.

MCP replaces this with a unified, open protocol. A developer builds an MCP server for their tool once, and any AI host application that supports the protocol can immediately use it.

How It Works (The Architecture)

MCP operates on a simple client-server model built over JSON-RPC 2.0:

[ User Interaction ]
        │
        ▼
   [ MCP Host ]  ◄──► [ LLM (Brain) ]
 (e.g., Claude, Cursor IDE)
        │
        ▼
  [ MCP Client ]
        │  (Communicates via JSON-RPC)
        ▼
  [ MCP Server ] ◄──► [ External Data / System ]
 (e.g., Postgres, GitHub, Local Filesystem)
  1. MCP Host: The main application or development environment the user interacts with (e.g., Cursor, Claude Desktop, VS Code plugins).
  2. MCP Client: A secure connector inside the host that manages communication with various servers.
  3. MCP Server: A lightweight, specialized program that exposes specific data or capabilities from a target tool.

Core Primitives: What Can an MCP Server Do?

MCP servers expose three fundamental elements to an AI model:

  • Resources: Data streams or text context that the AI can read (e.g., a file's contents, log entries, or a database schema).
  • Tools: Executable functions that allow the AI to take actions (e.g., running a terminal command, creating a GitHub issue, or executing a SQL query).
  • Prompts: Predefined templates or specialized workflows that help guide how the user and AI interact for specific tasks.

Why It Matters

Because major AI players (including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Microsoft Azure) support or track the standard, MCP has quickly become the foundation for Agentic AI. It transitions LLMs from passive text-generators into active assistants capable of safely navigating local directories, reading code bases, interacting with APIs, and performing complex multi-step workflows.

turns.prompt_text: So it's like gear grease, it makes it so that once a port to AI is created, nothing more is necessary for basic use
turns.response_html:
That is a perfect analogy. It is exactly like gear grease, or better yet, a universal physical coupling for gears.

Before MCP, every time you wanted to hook an AI up to a new machine, you had to custom-forge a completely unique gear to make the teeth mesh perfectly. If the AI changed or the machine upgraded, the teeth wouldn't line up anymore, and everything would grind to a halt.

With MCP:

  1. You attach a standardized "coupling" to the machine (the MCP Server).
  2. The AI application uses that exact same standard connection (the MCP Client).
  3. They click together instantly.

Once that interface is built, the AI can seamlessly turn the gears of that application for basic reading, writing, and executing actions without you ever having to write custom integration code again. It completely removes the friction of getting AI agents to talk to the software tools we use every day.

Hexagonal Architecture—also widely known as Ports and Adapters Architecture—is a software design pattern introduced by Alistair Cockburn in 2005.

Its core purpose is to isolate your core business logic from any outside technologies, frameworks, databases, or user interfaces.

Think of it as designing a universal engine. The engine doesn't care whether it’s being dropped into a sports car, a boat, or a lawnmower, nor does it care if the fuel comes from a premium tank or a temporary siphon. It just needs the right hookups to run.

The Core Concept: Inside vs. Outside

Instead of the traditional layered architecture (Presentation $\rightarrow$ Business $\rightarrow$ Database) where everything is tightly coupled to the database, Hexagonal Architecture splits the world into two clean halves:

  1. The Inside (The Core): This contains your domain models, business rules, and pure logic. It is completely technology-agnostic. There are no SQL queries, no HTTP routing frameworks, and no external API libraries here.
  2. The Outside (The Infrastructure): This is where the real world lives. It includes UI screens, REST endpoints, CLI tools, databases, cloud storage, and third-party services.

How It Connects: Ports and Adapters

To bridge the gap between the inside and the outside without letting them mix, the architecture uses two components:

1. Ports (The Inside's Interface)

A Port is an entry or exit point defined by the core application. In code, a port is almost always an Interface. It dictates the contract of how things must interact with the application, without knowing who is doing it.

  • Driver (Inbound) Ports: Interfaces that allow the outside world to trigger the core logic (e.g., a PlaceOrderUseCase interface).
  • Driven (Outbound) Ports: Interfaces that the core logic uses to talk to the outside world when it needs data or actions (e.g., an OrderRepository interface to save data).

2. Adapters (The Outside's Implementation)

An Adapter is the concrete implementation that glues an external technology to a specific port.

  • Driver (Inbound) Adapters: They take a request from the outside world, translate it, and call a port. Examples: A REST Controller, a GraphQL resolver, or a CLI command script.
  • Driven (Outbound) Adapters: They implement the port interface defined by the core to talk to specific infrastructure. Examples: A Hibernate/SQL class that talks to a Postgres database, or a mock class used for local testing.

Why Use It?

  • Total Testability: Because the core application has no hard dependencies, you can unit-test your entire business logic in milliseconds without spinning up a real database, web server, or cloud environment. You just pass in mock adapters.
  • Tech-Agnostic Flexibility: If you decide to swap your database from MongoDB to PostgreSQL, or change your communication layer from REST to gRPC, you only rewrite the adapters on the far edges. The core business logic remains completely untouched.
  • Protection Over Time: External frameworks go out of style, upgrade breaking changes, or get abandoned. By forcing them to stay on the outer rim of your hexagon, your critical business rules are safe from framework churn.

Why a hexagon? Cockburn chose the shape simply because it has enough sides to visually represent multiple inbound and outbound ports at the same time, busting the old mental model of top-to-bottom layers.

Would it help to see a quick code skeleton illustrating how a port and adapter interface look in practice?

This is a visualization of the Hexagonal Architecture, re-imagined as a modular space station. In this analogy:

  • The Inside: Your core business logic is the "Command Center" in the middle. It’s technology-agnostic; it only knows its own rules and the standard docks.
  • The Ports: These are the Universal Docking Bays (the green rings). They define the connection standard, but don’t care what ship connects to them.
  • The Outside: These are the various modules/ships (the adapters) that connect to fulfill specific needs. The Web Portal connects like any other UI, and the SQL database connects like any other storage.

This setup makes it perfectly testable: If you wanted to test the Command Center, you don't need a massive SQL storage unit; you can just plug a light, "mock" cargo crate into that same docking port.

turns.prompt_text: Cool, but this seems very simple, I don't understand how it's different from any of the other ones. Essentially, you're just saying use a plug-and-play methodology or a hub and spokes system where everything builds or connects to the core application
turns.response_html:
You are spot on: at a high level, it is just a hub-and-spoke or plug-and-play model. If it feels like common sense, that’s because modern software design has largely adopted its principles.

To see why Hexagonal was a revolutionary shift, you have to look at what it was fighting against: the traditional Layered (N-Tier) Architecture that dominated software for decades.

Here is where the true, fundamental difference lies.

The Old Way: Layered Architecture (Database-First)

In a traditional layered architecture, the application is built like a stack of pancakes.

   [ Presentation Layer ]  (UI / Web Controllers)
            │
            ▼
     [ Business Layer ]    (The Rules / Logic)
            │
            ▼
     [ Database Layer ]    (SQL / ORM / Data Access)

The Problem: Transitively Hooked to Infrastructure

Look at the direction of the arrows. The Business Layer depends directly on the Database Layer.

Because the code in your business logic explicitly calls database libraries or imports data-access objects, your core business rules are permanently glued to your storage technology. If you want to run a business rule, you must have a database connection active. If you swap MySQL for MongoDB, you have to tear open your business layer and rewrite it.

The Hexagonal Way: Dependency Inversion (Domain-First)

Hexagonal architecture flips those arrows completely using a concept called Dependency Inversion. The core business logic doesn't depend on anything outside of itself. Instead, the outside world depends on contracts (Ports) defined by the core.

       [ Outside ]                      [ Inside (The Core) ]

[ Web Controller (Adapter) ]  ───►    [ Driver Port (Interface) ]
                                                  │
                                                  ▼
                                      [ Business Logic / Domain ]
                                                  ▲
                                                  │
[ Postgres Repo (Adapter) ]   ───►    [ Driven Port (Interface) ]

The Difference: The Core is King

Notice the bottom arrow now. The Postgres Database Adapter points inward toward the Driven Port interface.

The core application simply says, "I have a rule that requires saving a user. I don't care how it happens. Here is an interface called UserRepository with a save() method." The database layer on the outside has to conform to what the core wants, not the other way around. The database becomes a trivial detail.

Why this isn't just "any other system"

While many patterns talk about decoupling, Hexagonal specifically enforces strict rules about code dependencies:

  • Zero Frameworks in the Core: In a hub-and-spoke model, the hub might still be built on a specific framework (like Spring Boot, Express, or Next.js). In Hexagonal, the core hexagon contains pure language code. No web annotations, no database decorators, no HTTP abstractions.
  • The "Right-Side" Isolation: It’s easy to see how a web UI plugs into an API (the left side). But Hexagonal treats the database, email servers, and third-party APIs (the right side) exactly the same way. The core doesn't know it's saving to a database; it just thinks it's sending data into a void that implements its interface.
  • Asymmetry of Intent: It distinguishes between what drives the application (users, cron jobs, test scripts) and what is driven by the application (databases, message queues). They plug in differently based on who holds the control flow, but both keep the center pristine.

In short: Other architectures decouple the front-end but leave the back-end business logic tightly chained to the database. Hexagonal Architecture cuts the chains on both sides, leaving your business logic floating safely in the center, completely oblivious to the tech stack running it.
